sense: games and physical exercise; a particular sport

terms.gloss: sport: the games and exercise of the Campus Martius
terms.grammar: noun, second declension, with an adjective
evidence: Suet. Aug. 83: exercitātiōnēs campestrēs equōrum et armōrum
terms.comment: The Roman sport was what the young did on the Campus Martius: riding, weapons, running, ball games, swimming in the Tiber. Suetonius calls them exercitātiōnēs campestrēs. Traupman and Morgan–Owens use campester for “sports”: vestis campestris, sportswear (Traupman 45).

terms.gloss: a game; with a genitive, one sport
terms.comment: For a game in general see game; for physical exercise, exercise.
Pliny’s word for the art of the professional athlete; Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for sport in general.
Traupman’s coinage from the English word. No ancient author has it, and the classical words above do its work.

phrases.latin: sibi habeant igitur arma, sibi equōs, sibi hastās, sibi clāvam et pilam, sibi natātiōnēs atque cursūs
phrases.english: so let the young keep their weapons, their horses and their spears, their club and ball, their swimming and running

phrases.latin: Exercitātiōnēs campestrēs equōrum et armōrum statim post cīvīlia bella omīsit et ad pilam prīmō folliculumque trānsiit
phrases.english: Straight after the civil wars he gave up riding and weapons practice on the Campus, and went over at first to ball games

phrases.latin: lūdere quī nescit, campestribus abstinet armīs, indoctusque pilae discīve trochīve quiēscit, nē spissae rīsum tollant impūne corōnae
phrases.english: a man who can’t play keeps away from the Campus: if he has no skill at ball or discus or hoop, he stays still, so that the crowded rings of onlookers can’t laugh at him with impunity
play sports, be involved in sports

phrases.latin: Diēbus prōfēstīs plērumque in āthlēticā versor.
phrases.english: On weekdays I am generally involved in sports.
